Over-the-top (OTT) advertising has transformed how brands engage TV audiences. Streaming services now offer access to premium content, precise targeting, and new ways to connect exposure to business outcomes. But this doesn’t guarantee strong performance—brands still need a strategic approach.
With viewers fragmented across platforms, advertisers need to wrangle growing complexities in media buying, frequency management, and measurement. The opportunity isn’t simply to expand reach, but identify where streaming delivers incremental value and develop a strategy that can prove it.
Let’s take a closer look at what it takes to turn OTT advertising into an accountable growth channel.
The Skinny
- OTT advertising extends television beyond traditional distribution. It delivers video ads over the internet across smart TVs, streaming devices, and mobile. Connected TV (CTV) refers to the television device environment within the broader OTT ecosystem.
- Start with business outcomes, not platforms. Awareness, consideration, and conversion require different audiences, creative approaches, and performance metrics.
- Choose the right buying model. Direct buying offers premium inventory access and content alignment, while programmatic buying provides flexibility and faster optimization.
- Measure incremental impact. Platform attribution alone can’t establish whether advertising generated additional business. Incrementality testing and cross-media measurement help separate actual growth from attributed results.
- Connect OTT to the broader media strategy. Tinuiti’s direct publisher relationships and integrated approach have helped brands like Sony and Chomps use streaming to support larger marketing objectives.
You need incremental measurement in 2027.
Incrementality can help marketers identify sources of ad waste and understand which touchpoints promote growth. Our playbook explains it all.
What OTT Advertising Means in Today’s Streaming Ecosystem
Gone are the days when TV advertising was confined to traditional cable, satellite, or broadcast networks. OTT advertising delivers video commercials over the internet through streaming services and apps, reaching viewers on smart TVs, smartphones, tablets, computers, and gaming consoles. Brands can advertise across ad-supported subscription services, free streaming platforms, broadcaster apps, and live television.
OTT is often used interchangeably with connected TV (CTV), but they aren’t quite the same thing. OTT describes how video content reaches audiences, while CTV refers to the devices they use to watch it. For example, viewers who stream Hulu on a smart TV use both OTT and CTV, while those watching on an iPhone use OTT alone.
Or, as the IAB Tech Lab explains, OTT and CTV represent different aspects of streaming, each with distinct considerations for inventory selection, creative, reporting, and measurement.
So what makes OTT particularly valuable for marketers?
It combines television’s premium sight, sound, and motion with data-driven targeting and digital measurement capabilities. Brands can target specific segments, coordinate campaigns across publishers, and evaluate performance against business objectives.
That flexibility, however, comes with its own complications.
Audiences are frequently spread across competing platforms, household-level identity can be unreliable, and publisher reporting doesn’t always provide a complete picture of performance. As connected TV adoption and streaming video consumption reshape viewing habits, advertisers need to reconsider how they allocate television budgets and measure reach. The challenge is turning those capabilities into measurable results. That requires three key ingredients:
- High-quality audiences
- A measurement strategy established before launch
- Sufficient investment to generate meaningful results
Build an OTT Advertising Strategy Around Business Outcomes
More targeting options and sophisticated measurement don’t automatically translate into better results. To make the most of OTT advertising, brands need to establish what they want to accomplish before deciding where or how to spend their budgets.
Identify the Role OTT Should Play
OTT doesn’t need to serve the same purpose for every brand. For some, streaming provides incremental reach beyond existing TV campaigns, but it can also help connect with particular segments, support launches, generate demand, or re-engage previous buyers. Common objectives include:
- Incremental reach: Engage audiences who aren’t exposed to existing TV or digital video campaigns
- Priority audience engagement: Deliver messaging to high-value customers, category prospects, or specific demographic segments
- Product launches: Build awareness and consideration among consumers most likely to purchase a new product
- TV efficiency: Improve audience precision and reduce unnecessary duplication across media investments.
- Measurable demand: Generate incremental website visits, leads, or purchases
- Re-engagement: Reconnect with existing customers or lapsed buyers through relevant messaging
The goal determines OTT’s role in your media mix, whether that’s extending reach, improving audience precision, testing new approaches, or supporting a full-funnel strategy. To more effectively evaluate performance, stick with one or two primary objectives before launch.
If you’re treating your 15-second short the exact same way you treat a two-hour podcast on that living room TV, you’re just going to be bleeding budget… you have to architect the buy very intentionally.
Brian Binder, Senior Director, TV, Audio & Display Innovation, Tinuiti
Translate the Objective Into KPIs
Once you’ve established what OTT needs to accomplish, decide how you’ll actually measure success.
Impressions, video completion rates, and cost per thousand impressions (CPM) help measure campaign delivery and efficiency, but they don’t necessarily show whether your ads changed consumer behavior. Similarly, platform-reported ROAS can be useful for optimization, but it doesn’t independently prove that sales wouldn’t have occurred without the campaign.
Be sure to separate operational metrics from business outcomes, and establish which measurement source you’ll use to evaluate performance.
As long as you can bring the appropriate framework for measurement and planning to this environment, you can really make all of these channels work for you at every stage of the funnel—including TV.
Harry Browne, VP of Innovation and Growth for TV, Audio & Display, Tinuiti
Define the Audience Before Selecting Platforms
It’s tempting to start with a popular streaming service and build a campaign around its targeting options, but you don’t put the platform ahead of the customer. Instead, start by identifying the segments most relevant to your campaign, such as high-value customers, category prospects, lapsed buyers, or consumers in expansion markets.
Next, evaluate the available data. First-party customer information can support more relevant targeting, but only if it’s accurate, current, permissioned, and sufficiently large to activate.
Also consider whether you can apply consistent audience definitions across publishers and measure reach when identity matching is incomplete.
With those foundations in place, media planners can evaluate which streaming services offer the right combination of inventory, targeting capabilities, and scale to reach those audiences.
OTT Ad Targeting and Buying Models
OTT advertising offers more audience selection options than traditional TV buying, but greater precision comes with trade-offs. Narrow targeting can limit scale, while fragmented inventory complicates frequency management. Your buying model also determines how much control you have over placements, data, and optimization.
Advertisers can combine several targeting approaches to balance audience relevance, scale, and privacy requirements:
First-party data targeting
Your own customer data is often a valuable starting point. Customer relationship management (CRM) records, loyalty programs, and permissioned website or app audiences can help brands identify high-value segments.
These data sources support acquisition, re-engagement, and suppression strategies. For example, a brand seeking new customers might exclude known purchasers from a prospecting campaign where reliable identity matching is available.
However, first-party data isn’t automatically ready for activation. It must meet applicable privacy and consent requirements, and advertisers should assess match rates, audience size, and data freshness before putting it to use.
Third-party and modeled audiences
Demographic, behavioral, and in-market segments help brands reach beyond their existing customer base. Modeled audiences can also identify potential customers with characteristics similar to those of high-value buyers. One caveat: methodologies vary among providers, so brands should understand how segments are constructed, refreshed, and validated.
Contextual and geographic targeting
Contextual targeting places ads alongside relevant programming, genres, or content categories, while geographic targeting focuses investment on particular regions or designated market areas (DMAs). Both approaches can complement identity-based targeting, particularly when privacy restrictions or limited identifiers reduce audience match rates.
Frequency management
Reaching the right audience is only half the battle. Advertisers also need to manage how often viewers see the same ad.
Individual publishers may enforce frequency caps within their own environments, but those controls don’t necessarily extend across competing platforms. Someone who streams across several services could encounter the same commercial repeatedly, even when each publisher stays within its own limits.
Advertisers should evaluate cross-platform frequency capabilities, deduplicated reach reporting, and opportunities to reduce excessive exposure. The goal isn’t maximum precision at any cost, but sufficient reach among relevant audiences without unnecessary spending.
Programmatic vs. Direct OTT Media Buying
Brands can purchase OTT inventory through direct publisher agreements, programmatic platforms, or a combination of both. The right choice depends on what you’re trying to accomplish, how much flexibility you need, and how much control you want over your media investment.
Direct media buying can be particularly valuable for major product launches, premium content partnerships, and campaigns requiring guaranteed inventory access. Advertisers negotiate directly with publishers, often securing greater control over placement, pricing terms, and custom opportunities.
Programmatic buying uses automated platforms to purchase available inventory across participating supply sources. This approach can simplify activation, support audience-based targeting, and enable more frequent adjustments. However, advertisers still need visibility into the supply path, intermediary fees, and placement transparency.
Hybrid buying combines direct publisher relationships with programmatic activation. A brand might secure premium inventory directly for a national awareness campaign while using programmatic buying to reach priority audience segments or support ongoing optimization.
Before committing investment, advertisers should ask three questions:
- Is inventory sourced directly from publishers or through intermediaries?
- Who controls access to campaign, placement, and exposure data?
- Can reach and frequency be measured across different supply sources?
These answers help advertisers evaluate their options for buying OTT advertising and determine which approach offers the right balance of reach, efficiency, and accountability. Ultimately, effective OTT media buying requires a clear understanding of where inventory comes from, how campaigns are managed, and how performance is measured.

Tinuiti Spotlight: Real Results From OTT Media Buying
Publisher relationships, creative execution, and measurement all influence how well streaming supports broader marketing objectives. Here’s what an effective OTT strategy looks like in practice:
Sony: Connecting Live Sports Advertising to Retail Sales
Sony transformed its Thursday Night Football advertising into a full-funnel campaign. Connecting its premium live sports reach with interactive shopping experiences, the strategy combined audience-specific creative, shoppable TV ads, and follow-up Amazon sponsored advertising to encourage purchases and measure performance across the customer journey. The campaign delivered measurable results:
- 65% of campaign-attributed sales came from new-to-brand customers on Amazon.
- 2X higher add-to-cart rate from an in-game retail promotion compared with Sony’s other Thursday Night Football games.
- 7% lift in brand favorability and 8% lift in brand consideration.
Video can deliver full-funnel performance. And brands that blend creativity with data-driven intelligence will lead the streaming revolution.
Bob Avellino, VP of Commerce Innovation, Tinuiti
Chomps: From Streaming TV to In-Store Sales
Chomps combined premium live sports inventory with interactive video ads, allowing viewers to add products directly to their Amazon carts. The meat snack brand then used Amazon Marketing Cloud to evaluate performance across online and in-store sales:
- 91% increase in units sold during the Thursday Night Football season opener compared with the previous week.
- 124% increase in units sold during an early Black Friday activation compared with the same day the previous week.
- 2X sales spike during Thursday Night Football games compared with the hour before kickoff.
- 98% of Thursday Night Football conversions occurred in-store.
Measure OTT Advertising Beyond Impressions
Brands need more than platform reporting to determine outcomes. A campaign can generate millions of impressions, strong completion rates, and favorable attributed ROAS, but that doesn’t mean it created incremental business value. So how do you effectively measure advertising performance?
Build a Measurement Hierarchy Before Launch
A measurement plan should establish data sources, reporting responsibilities, success thresholds, and evaluation methods before the campaign launches. From there, organize OTT measurement into three levels:
1. Delivery and quality
Start by confirming whether advertising ran as intended. Common metrics include impressions, completion rates, CPM, and invalid traffic. These indicators help identify delivery problems, evaluate inventory quality, and compare operational efficiency.
2. Audience reach and exposure
Determine who the campaign reached and how often. Key metrics include unique reach, incremental reach, average frequency, and audience overlap. These KPIs can indicate whether OTT reached new consumers or repeatedly exposed households already reached through other channels. They also support more efficient allocation across publishers.
3. Brand and business outcomes
Evaluate whether the campaign influenced the outcomes that justified the investment. Depending on objectives, these may include awareness, recall, incremental website visits, leads, purchases, or revenue.
This third level should carry the greatest weight in decisions about future investment.
Attribution, Incrementality, and Cross-Media Reach
Platform attribution provides useful information about conversions associated with advertising exposure. However, attribution models can overstate performance when multiple platforms claim credit for the same action or when customers would have converted without seeing an ad.
Incrementality testing helps advertisers determine how much additional business their campaigns actually generated. Depending on campaign scale and available data, you can use multiple approaches:
- Geographic holdout tests: Compare performance between exposed and unexposed markets.
- Matched-market tests: Evaluate similar geographic areas with different advertising conditions.
- Conversion lift studies: Compare outcomes between appropriately constructed exposed and control groups.
These methods can estimate the additional business impact attributable to advertising, although test design, sample size, and statistical power affect reliability.
Cross-media measurement introduces another challenge: a household may encounter the same brand across linear TV, streaming services, and online video. That means reach totals from each platform can double-count audiences and exaggerate campaign scale.
Deduplicated measurement provides a more accurate estimate of unique exposure across channels and reveals where additional investment can generate incremental reach. The IAB’s standardized measurement guidance for CTV and Nielsen’s cross-media measurement research also offer useful reference points for more consistent measurement practices.
Brands should also consider how brand lift studies complement conversion-focused analysis, particularly for campaigns designed to influence awareness and consideration over longer purchase cycles.

OTT Advertising Readiness Checklist
OTT can support a wide range of marketing objectives, but brands need the right foundations to invest effectively. Before committing significant budget, evaluate whether your organization has the strategy, audience data, creative assets, and measurement capabilities required to generate meaningful results.
How to Use the Scorecard
Rate each readiness category on a scale from 0 to 2:
- 0 = Not ready: The capability is missing or insufficient.
- 1 = Partially ready: Some requirements are in place, but improvements are necessary.
- 2 = Ready: The capability can support campaign activation and evaluation.
Interpret your score:
- 16–20: Ready for structured investment. The foundations are in place to develop and evaluate an OTT strategy.
- 10–15: Ready for a limited pilot. Address the most important deficiencies before scaling investment.
- 0–9: Build the foundations first. Focus on strategy, creative, data, and measurement before launching a significant campaign.
Even a high total score doesn’t eliminate critical launch requirements. A score of zero in strategic objective, creative quality, measurement infrastructure, or privacy and governance should be treated as a launch blocker until the issue is resolved.
If You’re Not Ready Yet
A low readiness score identifies where your brand needs to strengthen its capabilities before investing in OTT.
Start with four priorities:
- Improve first-party data quality. Review your customer records, audience definitions, consent processes, and activation capabilities. Prioritize data accuracy and usability over collecting additional information without a defined purpose.
- Develop two or three TV-ready creative concepts. Build assets that communicate a clear message, establish brand recognition, and suit the intended viewing environment. Follow best practices for creating and optimizing OTT ads and consider different creative approaches for awareness and response-oriented campaigns.
- Establish a cross-channel measurement baseline. Document existing reach, traffic, conversion, and sales performance. Identify which metrics will help determine whether OTT adds value beyond current media activity.
- Design a controlled pilot. Select a limited geography or audience segment, define success thresholds, and determine how results will inform future investment.
The purpose of a pilot is to generate evidence about audience response, creative effectiveness, and incremental impact, beyond simply confirming that OTT can deliver impressions.
Turn OTT Advertising Into an Accountable Growth Channel
OTT advertising gives brands more ways to reach streaming audiences, apply customer insights, and measure the impact of TV investment. Making the most of those opportunities requires a coordinated strategy built around clear business objectives.
Effective campaigns connect audience strategy, creative, media buying, and measurement to evaluate performance and guide future investment. The next step is to identify where OTT delivers incremental value, reduce unnecessary spending, and invest in the audiences, creative, and placements that produce meaningful results.
